content.text: JavaScript is a dynamically typed, single threaded, high-level, interpreted programming language that is primarily used to make web pages interactive and dynamic.
JavaScript allows developers to implement complex features on web pages, such as dynamically updating content, controlling multimedia, animating images, and much more.
How Does the Browser Understand JavaScript Code?
Browser first reads the HTML file and constructs a Document Object Model (DOM) tree. The DOM represents the structure of the web page.
When the browser encounters a <script> tag in the HTML, it
and starts loading and executing the JavaScript code within that script tag or from the external file linked via the src attribute.
After fetching the script, browser with the help of its built-in JavaScript engine

Once compiled, the JavaScript code is executed by the engine. The engine interacts with the DOM, Web APIs, and other parts of the browser to manipulate the web page as needed.
After JavaScript execution, if there are any changes to the DOM or CSS, the browser re-renders the affected parts of the web page.

questions.title: Why is JavaScript called a Single-Threaded language?

content.text: JavaScript is called a single-threaded language because it has a
, which means it can only execute one task at a time.
Due to this, JavaScript can only perform one operation at a time; it cannot execute multiple pieces of code simultaneously in the same thread.
Since JavaScript is single-threaded, if a piece of code takes a long time to execute (like a complex calculation or a blocking I/O operation), it can block the entire execution of the program.
To avoid this, JavaScript has asynchronous mechanisms like callbacks, Promises, and async/await to handle long-running operations without blocking the main thread.

JavaScript was designed to be single-threaded to simplify its execution model and avoid complex issues that arise in multi-threaded environments, such as race conditions, deadlocks, and thread synchronization.

questions.title: What is a call stack in Javascript?

content.text: Javascript manages execution context creation and deletion in the code execution phase with the help of
Call Stack maintains the order of execution of execution contexts.
First, the whole Global Execution Context (GEC) is pushed inside the stack. So, at the bottom of the stack we have GEC.
Whenever a new execution context is created by invoking a function this new execution context is pushed inside the stack and placed above GEC.
Once we are done with the execution of the function and returning its value, the execution context is moved out/deleted and control goes back to the GEC.
Same process will repeat for other functions.
After the whole program is executed, GEC is also deleted and the call stack gets empty.
After the call stack gets empty, the event loop pushes any async task waiting in the task queues into the call stack and it gets executed immediately.

questions.title: Explain shallow copy vs. deep copy and provide examples?

content.text: are concepts related to duplicating objects or arrays in JavaScript. They determine how nested objects within the original data structure are handled during the copying process.
Shallow copy is also identified as pass-by Reference.
In a shallow copy, only the top-level properties of the original object are copied to the cloned object.
If these properties are primitive values (like numbers, strings, or booleans), they are directly copied.
If the properties are references to nested structures (objects or arrays), only the reference address is copied, not the actual nested objects themselves.
So, original and cloned objects have the same reference to nested objects.
Thus, changes made to the nested objects in the one object will modify the other object.
Deep copy is also identified as pass-by Value.

When a deep copy of an object is created, all values including any nested objects are copied into cloned object by creating new references for each nested object. So, the original and the cloned objects have independent references to each nested value.
Thus, changes in the one object will not modify the other object.

Service Workers act as a programmable proxy between the browser and the network. It intercepts network requests made by the application and can modify them or serve responses from a cache, enabling features like offline access and improved load times.
Service workers can intercept network requests through the fetch event, and serve responses from the network, cache, or even generate responses programmatically.

By caching assets and data, service workers enable applications to work offline or with limited connectivity. - Particularly useful for creating "offline-first" applications that remain usable without an internet connection
They can also handle push notifications, enabling applications to receive updates even when they are not open in the browser.
Service workers can defer actions until the user is back online. e.g. saving form data when offline and allowing data to be sent to the server when connectivity is restored.

Once registered, the service worker enters the installation phase where it can cache resources. This phase can fail if there are issues with caching.
After successful installation, the service worker activates and takes control of all pages within its scope. It can then respond to fetch events and manage cached responses
When not actively handling events, the service worker may terminate to save memory but can be restarted when needed.
